full_judgment:
2. Instant Rule has been issued under section 25 of the Small Cause Courts Act, 1887, calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 17-6-2007 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Mymensingh, in SCC Suit No. 5 of 2003 should not be set aside and /or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 (c) The said house rent case was dismissed. However, on appeal, the said house rent case has been decreed, vide judgment and order dated 19-5-2013, passed in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 49 of 2007. 

 4. The Trial Court, after hearing the parties and having assessed the evince placed before it, has, by its judgment and decree dated 17-6-2007 has allowed the SCC suit No. 5 of 2003, on contest, and directed the defendant-petitioner to hand over the vacant premises to the plaintiff-opposite party, within 30 (thirty) days. 

 6. Learned Advocate Mr Subrata Shaha, appeared for the petitioner. He submits that the defendant is not a habitual defaulter as alleged by the plaintiff. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate has referred to a money receipt dated 18-2-2002 showing that an amount of Taka 3200 has been paid (as rent of 4 months) for the month of the January, February March and April of 2000 (Exhibit-Kha). He then referred to another money receipt dated 7-8-2002 (Exhibit-Kha 1) showing that the rent of May, June, July and August 2000 (4 months) has been paid, in lump. Learned Advocate further submits that, there is a practice of payment of rent in lump by and between the parties, therefore, the defendant cannot be treated as a habitual defaulter. He also submits that the landlord did not file or prove any plan approved by the concerned authority to show that he bonafide requires the suit premises for construction of any multistoried building on it. He emphatically argues that, mere plea of bonafide requirement is not sufficient and that the landlord should have adduced evidence to prove that he bonafide requires the suit premises. But, he next submits, the Trial Court, by decreeing the SCC Suit No. 5 of 2003, had utterly failed to assess the evidence placed before it and, therefore, he has arrived at wrong findings and committed error of law in passing the impugned judgment and decree, that has resulted in error in the impugned decision, occasioning failure of justice. He has relied upon 59 DLR (AD) 54: Jahanara Khatun vs Nazrul Islam, 15 BLD 119,: Munshi Amir Uddin Ahmed vs Begum Shamsunnahar and 40 DLR (AD) 1,: Golam Hossain vs Mst Asia Khatun, in support of his contention. He therefore, prayed that the Rule may be made absolute and that the impugned judgment and decree may be set aside. 

 7. Learned Advocate Mr. Abdul Hai Sarkar, appeared for the plaintiff-opposite party (landlord). He first of all refers to the agreement dated 1-9-1992 (Exhibit-Kha) and submits that this agreement was prepared by the defendant (tenant) and was signed by the plaintiff landlord on good faith, without going through the contents thereof, since, the defendant was a tenant under the plaintiff's father too. He next submits that, the defendant tenant has become a defaulter as admitted by him, during his cross-examination, being present as DW 1. He next points out that, as per clause 3 of the agreement dated 1-9-1992 (Exhibit-Kha), the defendant-petitioner (tenant) was bound to pay the rent of each month within 7 (seven) days of the next calendar month. But, he has admitted that he has defaulted on several occasions in payment of the rent within 7 (seven) days of the next month, as he was obligated to, under clause-3 of the agreement. Therefore, admittedly, the defendant-petitioner is a habitual defaulter and is liable to be evicted on this ground alone. The learned Advocate further submits that subsequent acceptance of rent by the landlord, paid beyond the due date, will not amount to waiver. Mere acceptance of rent, he continues, by the Landlord without objection or protest is not sufficient to constitute waiver and that, once the default occurs subsequent acceptance of the rent in lump, by the landlord, does not amount to waiver in the absence of any positive proof of his intention to waive such default. Payment of rent in lump does not save a tenant from the legal consequence justifying his eviction. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate has relied upon that cases reported in 40 DLR (AD) 89: Md Golam Hossain vs Mst Asia Khatun Chowdhury, 44 DLR (AD) 348: MG Jilani vs Md. Wahed Uddin Sardar. As regards the bonafide requirement for construction of multistoried building on the suit premises, the learned Advocate refers to the admission of the DW 1, made during his cross-examination, that, there are all multistoried buildings around the suit premises. The learned Advocate also submits that, this old one-storied building has to be demolished and new multistoried building has to be constructed for developing the suit property as has been done in all adjacent properties. He has, however, on query made from the Bench confirmed that, the monthly rent of Taka 600 and subsequently been raised to Taka 800 upon verbal agreement between the parties. He next submits that, as required under section 106 of the TP Act, the landlord has served a notice of eviction dated 1-3-2000, under register post, which was received on 1-3-2003 (exhibit-2). Therefore, the learned Advocate proceeds on, that the defendant was liable to be evicted on 1-3-2003 and the trial court, upon proper consideration of the oral and documentary evidence, has arrived at correct findings and has decreed the suit and that in passing the impugned judgment and decree, the Trial Court has committed no error of law. The learned Advocate further submits that, the plaintiff has filed the eviction suit in 2003 and that, after passing of the impugned judgment and decree on 17-6-2007, the defendant has filed the revisional application on 9-6-2007, now this is 2018. As such, the defendant is occupying the suit premises by filing this revisional application only to continue in the suit premises by dragging the matter and with a malafide intention to derive unjust benefit on payment of rents at a nominal rate. He continues that, this case is a clear abuse of process of the court, causing series prejudice to the plaintiff and that on these grounds the rule is liable to discharged with cost. 

 13. I have also considered the notice issued under section 106 TP Act, and I find that, by this notices (Exhibit-2), the tenancy has been terminated with the expiry of the end of the month of tenancy i.e. with effect from 1-3-2003 and, therefore, this notice has lawfully terminated the tenancy and the decree for eviction is well founded on the facts, circumstances and evidence on record. 

 The impugned judgment and decree passed by the Trial Court in SCC Suit No.5 of 2003, on 17-6-2007 is hereby up held, subject only to modification that the tenant will get 60 (sixty) days time to quit the suit premises, instead of 30 (thirty) days, and till then the defendant petitioner shall deposit the rent in the House Rent Control Suit No.1 of 2003.
